title: Integer to Roman
description: Brute force to optimized: greedily subtracting from a sorted list of denominations versus precomputed lookup tables for each of the four digit places.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer num, convert it to its Roman numeral representation, using the standard subtractive notation (such as IV for 4 and IX for 9).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given num, produce the Roman numeral string that represents it, following the standard convention where certain combinations, like IV or IX, subtract a smaller symbol placed before a larger one.

blocks.title: Analogy: Making Exact Change With a Fixed Set of Coin Values
blocks.text: Picture making change for an amount using a fixed set of coin denominations, some of which represent "subtractive" combinations (like a 9-cent coin, avoiding nine 1-cent coins); always use the largest denomination that still fits, then repeat with what remains.

blocks.caption: Roman numerals as a set of denominations, largest first, some subtractive

blocks.text: 3 is simply three I symbols in a row: III.
Before looping through every denomination for every digit, notice that Roman numerals are actually built independently, one digit place at a time.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The greedy approach, always subtracting the largest denomination that fits, works correctly because the chosen set of 13 values and symbols (including the subtractive ones like CM and IV) was specifically designed to make greedy subtraction always produce the correct, standard representation.

Observation 2: Each of the four digit places, thousands, hundreds, tens, and units, only ever has 10 possible values (0 through 9), and each one maps to a fixed, known Roman substring.

Observation 3: Since these four digit places never interact with each other, thousands only ever contributes M's, hundreds only ever contributes from a fixed list of 10 substrings, and so on, the whole numeral can be built by handling each place independently and concatenating the results.

Observation 4: This turns an iterative greedy search into 4 fixed table lookups, with no loop needed at all.
This leads to two valid strategies: greedily subtract from a sorted list of 13 denominations, or split num into its four digit places and look up each one directly.
Walk through a fixed list of value-symbol pairs, from largest to smallest, and while num is still at least the current value, append the symbol and subtract the value.

items: Store 13 (value, symbol) pairs in decreasing order: 1000/M, 900/CM, 500/D, 400/CD, 100/C, 90/XC, 50/L, 40/XL, 10/X, 9/IX, 5/V, 4/IV, 1/I.
For each pair, while num is at least that value, append the symbol to the result and subtract the value from num.
Move to the next pair once num is smaller than the current value.
Return the result once num reaches 0.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: greedily subtract the largest fitting denomination, repeating as needed

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The 13 denominations are listed strictly largest to smallest, including the subtractive combinations, so the greedy choice at each step is always correct.
The inner while loop handles a denomination being used more than once in a row, such as III needing the value 1 three times.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), since num is bounded by 3999 and at most a small constant number of symbols can ever be appended.
Space: O(1) beyond the fixed-size output string.

Limitation: the algorithm is already fast in practice, but it re-walks the denomination list and repeats a while loop for every single digit place, when each digit place actually only ever needs one direct answer out of 10 possibilities.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the greedy loop is not truly necessary: the thousands, hundreds, tens, and units digits of num never interact with each other in the final Roman string, each contributes its own independent, fixed chunk.

What are all the possible chunks: for hundreds, tens, and units, there are only 10 possible digit values, 0 through 9, each with one fixed, known Roman substring (for example, hundreds digit 9 always contributes CM).

What about thousands: since num never exceeds 3999, the thousands digit is 0 through 3, contributing 0 to 3 M symbols.

The core idea: precompute the 10 possible substrings for each digit place, then simply look up and concatenate the substring for each of num's four digits directly, no loop required.

Precompute 4 lookup tables, one for thousands (only 4 entries needed), and one each for hundreds, tens, and units (10 entries each). Extract each digit of num with division and modulo, look up its corresponding substring in the matching table, and concatenate all four results.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: one direct table lookup per digit place, no loop

codes.python:
def int_to_roman(num):
    thousands = ['', 'M', 'MM', 'MMM']
    hundreds = ['', 'C', 'CC', 'CCC', 'CD', 'D', 'DC', 'DCC', 'DCCC', 'CM']
    tens = ['', 'X', 'XX', 'XXX', 'XL', 'L', 'LX', 'LXX', 'LXXX', 'XC']
    units = ['', 'I', 'II', 'III', 'IV', 'V', 'VI', 'VII', 'VIII', 'IX']

    return (thousands[num // 1000]              # one direct lookup per digit place
            + hundreds[(num // 100) % 10]
            + tens[(num // 10) % 10]
            + units[num % 10])

blocks.text: Because the four digit places of a number under 4000 never interact in Roman numeral notation, thousands only ever produces M repeated up to 3 times, and each of hundreds, tens, and units maps to exactly one of 10 known substrings, precomputing those substrings and looking each one up directly reproduces the exact same result as the greedy approach, without any loop.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1), exactly 4 lookups and a concatenation, regardless of num.
Space: O(1) beyond the fixed-size lookup tables.

blocks.text: Integer to Roman has two equally valid solutions: greedy subtraction against a carefully chosen list of denominations, or direct lookup tables per digit place. Both rely on the same underlying fact, that the subtractive Roman notation was designed so the greedy approach always produces the standard, correct representation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid a loop entirely", think: precompute the 10 possible substrings for each digit place and look them up directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the greedy denomination approach and the digit-place lookup approach run in O(1) time and space, since num is bounded by 3999.

items: Pattern: greedy denomination matching, or equivalently, independent per-digit-place lookup tables.
Core Idea: the subtractive Roman denominations (CM, CD, XC, XL, IX, IV) make greedy subtraction always produce the correct standard form; each digit place can also be looked up independently.
Time: O(1) for both approaches, since num is bounded.
Most Important Observation: the four digit places of a number under 4000 never interact in Roman numeral notation, letting each be looked up independently.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the subtractive denomination set is known; a common one to have memorized in advance.
One line memory trick: greedily subtract the largest fitting denomination from a list that already encodes the subtractive rules.
